The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and enhances its emotional resonance. The actual "story time" covers only a few minutes—a brief conversation on a ferry dock and a short walk into the ferry house. However, the author skillfully stretches these moments by interspersing the sparse dialogue with rich sensory details (the dripping steel cable, the thumping hull, the suitcase wheels catching in the planks) and Ilse’s internal observations. This slow, deliberate pacing mirrors the quiet, stagnant life at the ferry crossing and emphasizes the unspoken tension and grief (implied by the presence of Henning's unused mug) between mother and son. 

At the same time, the author uses extreme time compression to provide necessary backstory without bogging down the narrative. Years of history, routine, and growing apart are compressed into single sentences—such as the motor coughing "for eleven years," or the flash of memory showing Jonas as a ten-year-old boy on the pier. This balance between the stretched, heavy present and the compressed past creates a poignant and immersive atmosphere.
